\begin{CRchronicle}{79}
The nineteenth day of Frost came on under the Vail roof by degrees and from the outside. The boy lay carried and awake, two hundred and eighty-eight days old by a count nobody kept, with one crust two inches off and the empty place beside it unnamed. He took the body as it presented itself — crust, gap, thread frozen in the dry heat, cold at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform. He wanted the crust lifted and could not close two inches on the pot handle. Both were true, and the second was louder.

Sella went to the fire before the basket, said \emph{The house will keep it}, turned the coals with a broken pot, kept the charcoal unread, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand and left the widow’s mark untouched, for a morning is not an opening. The yard went around its seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, and the stayed frost on the well lip and the silt-clouded plate of ice on its flat stone were called weather. In the afternoon an ownerless voice over the boards gave the Frost 14 saying a second shaping: what a runner carries in a slate that has a name in it. The boy filed it beside the first with a finger between, not making Hessa a reader and not letting two shapings stand up as a witness.

On the twentieth the district’s arithmetic changed a second time. Berr Clay wiped his thumb twice, read \emph{one in twelve} into the two hundred, sent the figure over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, called the levy and denied it with \emph{It is not called by me}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The subtraction went up in the locked box and could not be changed back; the figure read was still not the figure paid. Hessa carried his slate toward Greybank unread. Two sightings at the market, a cup turned a quarter and a half-turn after a knock, were a colour and a shape with no eighth.

On the twenty-first the house kept its small grammar. The boy came into his two hundred and ninety days, told by nobody; the hand held an intake past its letting-go and through the little silence, left it whole and empty, then set the held interval beside the empty interval with a finger between and came down on the river’s note. One hundred and fifty-six answers stood exact and worth nothing at two inches of air. The hand laid back against the fold, 290 stood spoken by nobody, and the river went quiet. Nothing was opened, named, called, paid or ended.
\end{CRchronicle}
